definition: Duress means unlawful pressure or threats used to force someone to act.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word duress. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know duress should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Historians note that the border treaty was sealed under duress, with the enemy's army camped within sight of the palace walls.
Pressure is far milder than duress — deadlines, expectations, and insistent asking can all lean on you without any threat behind them.
Intimidation is a shade weaker than duress — the fear is real, but duress is the legal term for pressure so improper that a signature given under it does not count.

Coercion is the act of forcing someone — what the threatener does, seen from the threatener's side. Duress is the same event seen from the victim's side: the unlawful pressure they were under, which is why the law says a signature given under duress does not bind.

Extortion is the crime of squeezing money or favors out of someone by threats — it names what the criminal is after. Duress names the victim's condition: pressure so improper that the law treats whatever was agreed under it as never truly chosen.

In 1911, the schooner Alma Kane lost her rudder in a gale off the cape, and the only tug in sight ran up a signal: help for half the cargo.
Captain Reyes signed the tug's paper with the storm still breaking over his deck and his crew lashed to the rails.
In court the next spring, his lawyers argued the agreement had been made under duress — consent in name only, with the sea itself standing in for the threat and the tug's master making use of it.
The admiralty judge agreed, and the famous half-cargo contract was set aside.
A signature, the ruling said, is only as free as the hand that gives it.
